name: Long-Head Biceps Tendinopathy
summary: Anterior shoulder pain associated with loading of the long-head biceps tendon; frequently coexists with rotator cuff or labral pathology.

image.title: Rotator cuff and shoulder muscle anatomy

looksLike: Pain with resisted elbow flexion or supination
Pain during overhead or pulling activity
redFlags: Acute traumatic loss of strength or suspected rupture
Marked deformity/Popeye sign with acute pain
firstSteps: Modify painful overhead and heavy supination loads
Explain tendon load management and avoid complete rest

assess: Bicipital groove tenderness may be present
Shoulder ROM may be near full

tests.name: Uppercut Test
tests.purpose: Load the long-head biceps and reproduce familiar anterior shoulder pain.
tests.positive: Familiar anterior shoulder pain or painful weakness.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Modify painful overhead and heavy supination loads
Explain tendon load management and avoid complete rest
dose: Pain-tolerable isometric elbow flexion/supination: 4–5 x 20–30 seconds
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progressive elbow flexion/supination and shoulder strengthening
Train rotator cuff and scapular capacity
dose: Biceps curls and supination: 3 x 8–15, 2–3 days/week
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Graded return to throwing, lifting or occupational overhead tasks
Increase speed, volume and load separately
dose: Overhead/throwing progression with rest between higher-load sessions
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Overhead and pulling tasks completed without meaningful next-day flare

structures: Long-head biceps tendon in the bicipital groove and intra-articular segment
Rotator cuff and superior labrum may be associated
mechanism: Rapid increase in pulling, throwing or lifting volume
classification: Possible instability, partial tear or associated labral/rotator cuff disorder
investigations: Imaging is not routinely required for typical load-related pain.
Ultrasound/MRI or orthopaedic assessment when rupture, instability or significant associated pathology is suspected.
manual: Soft-tissue or shoulder mobility techniques may be used for short-term symptom modulation.
Do not repeatedly compress or aggressively friction a sensitive tendon.
modalities: No modality has been shown to replace progressive loading.
Consider short-term symptom relief only where it enables activity.
mistakes: Diagnosing isolated biceps disease from groove tenderness alone
pearls: Biceps symptoms often coexist with other shoulder disorders.
Load progression should reflect both shoulder and elbow demands.

tests.name: Uppercut Test
tests.purpose: Load the long-head biceps and reproduce familiar anterior shoulder pain.
tests.positive: Familiar anterior shoulder pain or painful weakness.
tests.patientPosition: Seated; elbow flexed 90°, forearm supinated; clinician resists an upward fist/uppercut motion.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Test clusters and associated cuff/labral findings are needed; no single biceps test confirms pathology.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
